experiment: Trip 2c: how long can the CPU be away from the drive between firmware polls? A spin of svc microseconds after every poll inside a 32-sector PIO read, at FAD 45150.

inputs.note: two complete bench runs in one saved log; the on-screen log wraps at 76 characters and was re-joined for parsing

hardware.disc: Not named in the report. The TOC (tracks at FAD 150 / 1076 / 45150, lead-out 549300) matches Sword of the Berserk, as in t1-ui-census-2026-09-19.json.
hardware.note: CMD 24 FAILED sense=6/40 at the start of a run is the drive's first INIT after a disc change, not an error.

slice_bytes_of_cpu_work.note: CPU work that fits in one slice at the measured rates (ui_hz=0): SD write 1180 KiB/s, SHA-256 2480 KiB/s

conclusions: Reads lose 0.1% to 2.3% at 1 ms of CPU-away time per poll, 0.7% to 7.4% at 4 ms (the two runs differ because their svc=0 baselines differ), and 18.5% to 24.1% at 10 ms.

The svc>0 rates are consistent between runs (spread 0.9% at 4 ms, 0.9% at 10 ms); the svc=0 rate is not (7.9% apart). So the loss at 4 ms is somewhere between 0.7% and 7.4%, and at 10 ms it is a clear 18.5-24.1%.

Consequence for the design: a single-threaded pipeline that does at most about 4 ms of SD-write or hash work between polls of the drive costs little (SD write moves about 1.2 KB per ms and SHA-256 hashes about 2.5 KB per ms, so a 4 ms slice is roughly 4.8 KB written or 10.0 KB hashed); a slice of 10 ms costs about a fifth of the read rate. This is the cooperative-interleave regime of the plan's decision table, with a small penalty, not a thread-only regime.
This measures the drive's tolerance only. Whether the SD write can be cut into 4 ms slices cheaply is a separate question for Trip 3 (small write sizes).

limitations: One card, one disc, one console; two runs; the svc=0 baseline moved 8% between them, which is larger than the effect at 1 ms and 4 ms.
ui_hz=1, so the UI took 1.4-3.6% of the CPU in these runs.
